name: Tara Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Tara, thanks for fitting me in. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't connected to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, what does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for a small builder doing extensions and loft conversions in a commuter town, three of us plus the boss, Keith. Right now we're building a kitchen extension for a couple who both work from home and come out every hour to ask how it's going. I do the carpentry: the roof, the stud walls, the loft floors, the stairs up into the loft. At lunch I'm on my phone using AI to draw up a garden room design for one of my own weekend customers.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Your own customers? Tell me about that, and what you like and don't like about the work.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I build garden rooms and decks at weekends, under my own name, mostly for people from church and their friends. I love the moment a customer walks into something I drew on my phone on Tuesday and built on Saturday. What I don't like is that Keith pays below the going rate, and there's not much else nearby, so the weekend work is how we get by. Dan drives a forklift in the big warehouse by the motorway, and between the mortgage, Noah and Ruby, and the tools I keep buying, there's never more than a few weeks in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool, and anyone who isn't using it is missing out. I'd keep telling people at church and on site how I use it to design and price. I'd probably post a before-and-after of a garden room I designed with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fine, maybe a little bit ahead. I already use it every day to quote faster and show customers drawings, so I'd keep that edge. It's not changing the world, but it's changing my weekends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I'm doing, and push the weekend business a bit harder. Maybe get some proper signage on the van and use the AI to run some local adverts. I'd still be cautious about leaving Keith's until the weekends pay as well as the weekdays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Quite cheerful, actually, as nothing gets in the way of my plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned buying tools. Is that part of why savings are thin?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A big part, yes. Last year I bought a mitre saw and a track saw on finance for the garden rooms. Dan raised an eyebrow, but I'd rather own my tools than have money sitting in a bank doing nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does Keith feel about the weekend business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He doesn't mind as long as I don't nick his customers. He's old school, writes quotes on carbon paper. I keep offering to show him the AI, and he keeps telling me he's too old to learn tricks.

S0.say: AI is a useful tool and anyone not using it is missing out. She'd keep showing people at church and on site, and post a before-and-after of a garden room she designed with it.
S0.think: She'd be fine and maybe a little ahead, already using AI every day to quote and draw for customers. It isn't changing the world, but it is changing her weekends.
S0.do: Keeps her day job and pushes the weekend garden room business harder, adding van signage and AI-written local adverts. Stays at her employer until the weekends pay as well as weekdays.
S0.feel: Calm and quite cheerful, as nothing gets in the way of her plans.
S0.quote: It's not changing the world, but it's changing my weekends.
S0.fieldNote: Tara is entrepreneurial and an enthusiastic daily AI user, with a side business built through her church network. Her thin savings partly reflect her choice to invest in tools. She's confident but still cautious about leaving her steady job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change is coming, so get ahead of it rather than complain about it. Those who adapt will do well. I'd say people should look after themselves and their families, not wait for the government to sort it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's good for me. If the machines can do the heavy, repetitive bits, I can do more of the design and the customer side, which is what I'm best at. Small builders like me could take on bigger jobs with less help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start looking at the new kit as soon as it appears, a robot that cuts timber to a design, or one that helps lift panels. I'd save up for one, maybe lease it, for the weekend business. I'd also learn more of the AI design side, so I'm the one customers come to for something special.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit excited. I'd be worried about Dan, but for me it looks like a chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be worried about Dan. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Warehouses are where the robots always show up first, on the news anyway. If they automate his job, we lose the steady wage. That's when my weekend business stops being a nice extra and starts being the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people should look after themselves, not wait for government. What about people who can't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then their families and churches should help, and the government only where there's no one else. I've seen what the church does for people in a bad patch. It's more personal and it gets people back on their feet.

S1.say: Change is coming, so people should get ahead of it rather than complain; those who adapt will do well, and families should look after themselves rather than wait for government.
S1.think: It's good for her: if machines do heavy repetitive work, she can focus on design and customers, and small builders could take on bigger jobs with less help.
S1.do: Looks at new kit as soon as it appears, saving to buy or lease a cutting or lifting robot for her weekend business. Builds up her AI design skills to offer customers something special.
S1.feel: Calm and a little excited, though worried about her partner's warehouse job.
S1.quote: That's when my weekend business stops being a nice extra and starts being the plan.
S1.fieldNote: Tara sees Steady Disruption as an opening for her small business. Her main worry is her partner's warehouse job, which shows how the household is exposed. Her views favour family and church support over government help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a shock, but complaining won't help, so get moving. The government should keep things stable, but mostly people need to adapt fast and help each other. I'd say it at church, and I'd be offering to help others work out what to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, two years is scary even for me. If AI and robots can do the whole job, including design, then my edge disappears, and big companies with money will buy the robots first. With a few weeks of savings and Dan's job probably going too, we'd be in trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That first week, I'd sit down with Dan and cut back hard, no new tools, no holidays. I'd try to lease a robot for the weekend business before the big firms snap them all up, and pitch myself to local customers as the person who knows both the old way and the new kit. I'd also ask Keith if he'd go in on it with me, because two small firms together have a better chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. My mind would be racing, but I'd feel like I still have some moves left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use those two years before it arrives for anything in particular?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grow the weekend business as fast as I could, build up a list of loyal customers, and learn everything about the robots. Two years is enough to get a head start if you start the day you hear the news. It's not enough if you wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Keith is 'too old to learn tricks'. Would he go in with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if I did the robot side and he did what he knows, the planning rules and the old houses. He's stubborn, but he's not stupid. And he'd rather work with me than be put out of business by some national firm.

S2.say: It's a shock, but complaining won't help, so people should get moving. Government should keep things stable, but mostly people must adapt fast and help each other; she'd offer help at church.
S2.think: Two years scares even her: if AI and robots can design and build, her edge disappears and big companies will buy robots first. With weeks of savings and Dan's job likely going too, they'd be in trouble.
S2.do: Cuts back hard with Dan, leases a robot for the weekend business before big firms buy them all, and pitches herself as knowing both old and new ways. Asks her boss to team up with her.
S2.feel: Anxious, mind racing, but still with moves left.
S2.quote: Two years is enough to get a head start if you start the day you hear the news.
S2.fieldNote: Even under pressure, Tara's instinct is to act, bringing in robots herself and forming an alliance with her old-school boss. Thin savings and her partner's exposed job are what keep her anxious. She frames help in terms of community rather than the state.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a decent amount of time to get ready, so start now. Small businesses should be helped to buy the machines, not crushed by the big firms. And people should learn new skills now instead of waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years feels like a real opportunity. I could build up the business, get a robot, train Dan to help with it, and be ready when it fully lands. I'd still be worried about the money, but I'd feel more in control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd save hard, maybe a hundred a month from the weekend jobs, towards leasing a robot. I'd do a course on robot operation and design software, evenings. And I'd talk to Dan about leaving the warehouse in a couple of years and joining me, so we're not both depending on someone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly excited. There's money worries, but I can see the path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes for you between two years and five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years, I'm rushing and hoping. With five, I can build it properly. It's the difference between a garden room thrown up in a weekend and one with proper foundations.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd ask Dan to leave a steady job. Isn't that a risk with thin savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, but in this picture his steady job isn't steady. I'd rather we jumped together onto something we own than wait for the warehouse to give him a letter. We'd pray about it, mind, and talk it through with the kids.

S3.say: Five years is a decent time to get ready, so start now: small businesses should be helped to buy machines rather than crushed by big firms, and people should learn new skills now.
S3.think: Five years is a real opportunity: build up the business, get a robot, train Dan to help, and be ready on arrival. Money is still a worry, but she'd feel more in control.
S3.do: Saves around a hundred a month from weekend work toward leasing a robot and takes evening courses in robot operation and design software. Plans for Dan to leave the warehouse and join her within a couple of years.
S3.feel: Uneasy but mostly excited, with money worries and a visible path.
S3.quote: It's the difference between a garden room thrown up in a weekend and one with proper foundations.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets Tara turn her side business into a family business plan. Her imagery comes straight from her trade. Faith and family discussions shape even her riskiest decisions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so use it. Learn the new tools, build something of your own, and look after your family. The government should keep things fair for small businesses, and then stay out of the way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years sounds like the best version for me. I'd have time to build the business properly, bring Dan in, buy the robots when they get cheaper, and maybe even take on an apprentice. By then Noah and Ruby would be older, maybe even working with us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first couple of years, I'd grow the weekend business and save for kit. I'd learn the robot and design side properly, and I'd pick the moment to leave Keith's when the weekends pay enough. I'd talk to Noah about whether he wants to join the business, or learn something that fits alongside it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. It feels like a long road, but a road I want to be on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that worries you, even with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the big firms buy up all the robots and undercut everyone, like the supermarkets did with the corner shops. Ten years is enough for me, but it's also enough for them. I'd want to get in early and build loyal customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Noah and Ruby?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to work hard, learn the new tools, and never be afraid to build something of their own. Noah's already good with his hands. Ruby's a little organiser, she'd probably end up running the business and telling me off.

S4.say: Ten years is a gift to be used: learn new tools, build something of your own and look after family. Government should keep things fair for small businesses and otherwise stay out of the way.
S4.think: Ten years is the best version for her: time to build the business properly, bring Dan in, buy robots as they get cheaper and maybe take on an apprentice, with the children possibly joining.
S4.do: Grows the weekend business and saves for kit in the first couple of years, learns robot and design skills, and leaves her employer once weekends pay enough. Talks with her son about joining the business.
S4.feel: Calm, on a long road she wants to be on.
S4.quote: Ruby's a little organiser, she'd probably end up running the business and telling me off.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Tara's picture is almost entirely hopeful and centred on a family business. Her one fear is big firms buying up robots and undercutting small builders. Her free-market, family-first views run consistently through every answer.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no time to build anything solid and the big firms would get the robots before anyone small. What would help is cheap loans or leasing deals for small builders to get the machines, and fair rules so the big national firms can't undercut everyone into the ground.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the customers. People still want to look someone in the eye before they let them build in their garden. That trust is what I'm really selling, and no robot's going to have a cup of tea with Mrs Hill after church.

headlineQuote: That trust is what I'm really selling, and no robot's going to have a cup of tea with Mrs Hill after church.
portrait: Tara Fischer is a 43-year-old extension and loft carpenter who runs a weekend garden room business through her church network, uses AI every day to design and price, and keeps her savings thin by buying tools. She stays calm in AI Plateau and Steady Disruption, seeing a chance to grow her own business with robots. AGI by 2028 makes her anxious because her savings are thin and her partner's warehouse job is exposed, but she still moves first, leasing a robot and teaming up with her boss. With five or ten years she plans a family business with her partner and perhaps her children. She favours family, church and small business over government help.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because there'd be no time to build anything solid and big firms would get the robots first.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap loans or leasing deals for small builders to get the machines, and fair rules so big national firms can't undercut everyone.
